_note: Each risk's score = sum of matched weights. Ranking = descending score. Top 7 shown by default. kb_url paths follow library.airiskpractice.org/docs/ structure.

relevance_template.default: Overreliance risk in any consequential AI system; operators must understand model limitations.
relevance_template.financial_services: Credit officers or decisioning systems may systematically defer to model outputs without independent review, especially when performance looks good.
relevance_template.healthcare: Clinicians face known automation bias with AI diagnostic tools — the model's confidence can override clinical judgement.
relevance_template.hr_employment: HR staff relying on AI screening scores without independent evaluation risk perpetuating systematic errors.

relevance_template.default: Model performance degrades silently as the world changes; monitoring cadence and drift thresholds are essential.
relevance_template.financial_services: Credit conditions, applicant populations, and macroeconomic state all shift. A model accurate at deployment may not be accurate 18 months later.
relevance_template.healthcare: Patient populations and clinical practice evolve; models trained on historical cohorts may silently diverge.

relevance_template.default: Metrics that look good on test sets can hide real-world failure modes; evaluation methodology needs independent scrutiny.
relevance_template.financial_services: Model evaluation on historical approved loans systematically understates performance on the full applicant population.

relevance_template.default: Inability to explain individual decisions damages trust and creates regulatory exposure.
relevance_template.financial_services: Article 86 (EU AI Act) right to explanation and GDPR Article 22 require meaningful explanations for credit decisions. Customer disputes are guaranteed without this capability.
relevance_template.healthcare: Clinician trust requires understanding why a model flagged a case; opaque outputs undermine adoption and safety.
relevance_template.hr_employment: Unexplainable hiring or promotion decisions face legal challenge and erode employee trust.

relevance_template.default: Cross-functional AI systems split accountability between teams; explicit ownership must be assigned.
relevance_template.financial_services: Credit decisioning crosses risk, legal, model-ops, and business lines. Article 26 deployer obligations require named ownership — fragmented accountability is a direct regulatory exposure.
relevance_template.public_sector: Government AI systems face particularly severe accountability gaps — Robodebt-style outcomes arise when no single accountable owner exists.

relevance_template.default: Missing model documentation creates audit gaps and hampers incident response.
relevance_template.financial_services: EU AI Act technical documentation requirements for high-risk systems are substantial; retrofit is expensive.

relevance_template.default: Once deployed, retiring or replacing an AI system is operationally hard; lock-in is a foreseeable risk from day one.
relevance_template.financial_services: Credit models embed in downstream systems and processes; technical debt accumulates quickly.

relevance_template.default: Adversarial inputs can systematically manipulate model outputs; robustness testing is required.
relevance_template.financial_services: Credit scoring models are targets for applicant gaming — adversarial robustness testing is part of Article 15 obligations.

relevance_template.default: Prompt injection is the highest-priority security risk for LLM systems; OWASP LLM01.
relevance_template.financial_services: Customer-facing LLMs processing financial data are high-value targets for prompt injection attacks designed to exfiltrate data or trigger unauthorised actions.

relevance_template.default: Training data contamination can systematically corrupt model outputs; data pipeline integrity controls are required.
relevance_template.financial_services: Training data for credit models sourced from historical decisions can encode past discriminatory practices.

relevance_template.default: Training data quality determines model quality; representativeness gaps create systematic failure modes.
relevance_template.financial_services: If the training set under-represents thin-file applicants, low-income suburbs, or recent migrants, performance disparities follow. Article 10 data governance obligation.
relevance_template.healthcare: Clinical training datasets often under-represent minority populations, women, and rare conditions.
relevance_template.hr_employment: Historical hiring data encodes past biases; models trained on it learn to replicate them.

relevance_template.default: LLM systems can leak training data or contextual PII in responses; OWASP LLM02.
relevance_template.financial_services: Customer correspondence and financial data in LLM context windows are high-value disclosure targets.

relevance_template.default: Using personal data for AI training or decisioning may exceed the original consent basis; legal basis must be established.
relevance_template.financial_services: Using customer transaction data for credit model training requires clear legal basis under GDPR and Privacy Act.

relevance_template.default: Bias risk is present in any consequential decision system; disparate impact testing is essential.
relevance_template.financial_services: Credit scoring on protected-attribute-adjacent feature spaces (postcode as race proxy) is well-documented to encode disparate impact. Highest-priority risk for this configuration.
relevance_template.hr_employment: Hiring and promotion decisions are a heavily-litigated bias surface; EU AI Act Annex III §4 and US EEOC guidance both apply.
relevance_template.public_sector: Government AI decisions on benefits or eligibility directly harm vulnerable populations if biased.

relevance_template.default: Proxy variables can carry protected attribute information even when direct attributes are excluded.
relevance_template.financial_services: Postcode, spending patterns, and social network data can all carry race or socioeconomic proxies in credit models.

relevance_template.default: Systems deployed for one purpose gradually expand to adjacent uses without re-evaluation.
relevance_template.financial_services: Credit scoring models are often repurposed for fraud detection, marketing, or collections — each a different regulatory context.

relevance_template.default: Employees use unauthorised AI tools alongside sanctioned ones, creating data governance and liability gaps.
relevance_template.financial_services: Customer data uploaded to consumer AI tools by staff is a growing privacy and regulatory exposure.

relevance_template.default: Over-reliance on a single vendor creates continuity, pricing, and contractual governance risks.
relevance_template.financial_services: APRA CPS 230 material service provider obligations require documented exit plans and concentration risk management.

relevance_template.default: Sector-wide use of similar AI models creates correlated failure risk; systemic exposure is a macro-prudential concern.
relevance_template.financial_services: Multiple banks using similar credit scoring models from shared vendors creates correlated credit allocation that can amplify economic cycles.

relevance_template.default: AI decisions create the training data for future AI decisions; feedback loops amplify initial biases.
relevance_template.financial_services: Credit denials create thin files; thin files cause future denials; the cycle entrenches exclusion.

relevance_template.default: LLMs generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect content; hallucination risk must be mitigated before deployment.
relevance_template.financial_services: A financial advice or support chatbot hallucinating regulatory requirements or product terms creates direct legal and customer harm.
relevance_template.healthcare: Hallucinated clinical information from a medical AI is a patient safety issue.

relevance_template.default: Proprietary models can be extracted through systematic querying; IP and security controls are required.
relevance_template.financial_services: A credit scoring model is a proprietary competitive asset; model extraction exposes the scoring logic to gaming.

relevance_template.default: AI systems that only work well for digitally literate users exclude vulnerable populations.
relevance_template.public_sector: Government AI that requires digital access or literacy creates exclusion for populations most dependent on public services.

relevance_template.default: Vendor AI systems acquired without AI-specific due diligence import risks the organisation cannot see.
relevance_template.healthcare: Procured clinical AI without model documentation, validation data, and bias testing creates safety and regulatory exposure.
relevance_template.financial_services: EU AI Act Article 25 and APRA CPS 230 both require deployers to manage vendor AI as part of their own governance.

relevance_template.default: AI incidents require specialist response capabilities that most incident response plans do not currently address.
relevance_template.financial_services: EU AI Act Article 73 requires serious incident reporting within prescribed periods; without an AI-specific incident response plan, notification deadlines will be missed.

relevance_template.default: AI systems designed for legitimate purposes can be redirected for harmful uses.
relevance_template.generative_content: Generative AI systems can be misused to create disinformation, fraud material, or harmful synthetic content.

relevance_template.default: Every MCP server an agent connects to is a potential attack surface for injection, exfiltration, and supply chain compromise. Allowlisting and response sandboxing are required before deployment.
relevance_template.financial_services: Agentic systems connecting to financial data sources via MCP are high-value targets; a compromised MCP server can exfiltrate customer data or initiate unauthorised transactions.

relevance_template.default: In multi-agent pipelines, a successful injection at any agent propagates through inter-agent trust relationships to agents with broader permissions. Zero-trust between agents and chain-level audit logging are required.
relevance_template.financial_services: Multi-agent financial workflows (intake → analysis → action) create injection chain risk where a low-privilege agent can direct a high-privilege agent to initiate transactions or exfiltrate data.

relevance_template.default: Computer-use agents operating browsers can be hijacked by any webpage they visit via visual prompt injection. Sandboxed execution, domain allowlists, and human approval gates for irreversible actions are required.
relevance_template.financial_services: Browser-operating agents with access to financial systems or customer data are high-value hijacking targets; a single compromised webpage can redirect the agent to exfiltrate data or submit unauthorised forms.

relevance_template.default: Conventional application logs don't capture the reasoning chains and inter-agent message flows needed to audit agentic decisions. EU AI Act Art. 12 logging requirements apply; standard APM tooling is insufficient.
relevance_template.financial_services: Regulators require the ability to reconstruct AI-assisted compliance or credit decisions. Agentic systems without chain-level audit logging cannot satisfy this requirement.
relevance_template.healthcare: Clinical AI agents must produce audit trails sufficient to support investigation of adverse outcomes; standard logs won't capture why an agent took a specific clinical action.

risks.title: Irreversibility & Scope Creep in Autonomous Systems

relevance_template.default: Agentic systems can take irreversible actions (send, delete, pay, post) and accumulate scope beyond their intended boundaries. Human approval gates for irreversible actions and least-privilege permissions are required before deployment.
relevance_template.financial_services: An agent with payment or data access capabilities can initiate financial transactions or disclose data outside its intended scope; these actions may be unrecoverable. OWASP LLM06 Excessive Agency.
relevance_template.healthcare: An agent with access to clinical records or communication systems can take actions affecting patient care that cannot be undone; strict scope controls are essential.

relevance_template.default: Without an enterprise-wide policy governing autonomous AI action, individual agent deployments accumulate capabilities that collectively exceed what governance controls can manage. OWASP LLM06. An AI agent registry and action classification policy are required.
relevance_template.financial_services: Agents deployed across business units with heterogeneous permission sets create action chain risks — sequences of individually permitted actions that together produce prohibited outcomes such as data exfiltration or unauthorised payments.
relevance_template.public_sector: Government AI agents with broad administrative access and minimal oversight create accountability and legality risks when they take actions outside their defined mandate.
